rejected.title: The fall of Singapore and prisoners of war
card: Singapore was Britain's main base in South-East Asia. Japanese forces pushed down the Malay Peninsula, and on 15 February 1942 the British commander surrendered Singapore.
About 15,000 Australians were captured. They became prisoners of war (POWs): members of the armed forces held by the enemy.
Japan used many POWs as forced labour. On the Burma-Thailand Railway, prisoners cut a line through jungle and rock, mostly with hand tools.
Starvation, diseases such as cholera, overwork and beatings killed thousands of prisoners. Many who survived came home with lasting health problems.
rejected.remember: Singapore's surrender made about 15,000 Australians POWs, and thousands died in Japanese captivity.

a.q: Which statement about the fall of Singapore is correct?
opts: Japan took it, and about 15,000 Australians became POWs
Japan took it, and most Australians escaped by sea
Australia held it, and about 15,000 Japanese became POWs
Japan bombed it, but the Allied forces kept control
a.why: Japan took Singapore in February 1942, and about 15,000 Australians there became prisoners of war. Escaping by sea is tempting, but most Australians could not leave and were captured.
a.clue: Think about what a surrender means for the soldiers in a city.

b.q: Jim was captured at Singapore and sent to work on the Burma-Thailand Railway. Which best describes the conditions he faced?
opts: Forced labour with little food, and disease
Paid work with good food and medical care
Fighting as a soldier against Japanese troops
Guarding Japanese prisoners near the railway
b.why: On the railway, prisoners did forced labour with little food, and diseases such as cholera spread. Fighting as a soldier does not fit, because POWs had been captured and were made to work.
b.clue: Think about how Japan used its prisoners.

version.title: The fall of Singapore and prisoners of war
card: Singapore was Britain's main base in South-East Asia. Japanese forces advanced down the Malay Peninsula, and on 15 February 1942 the British commander surrendered Singapore.
About 15,000 Australians were captured there. They became prisoners of war (POWs): members of the armed forces held by the enemy.
Japan used many POWs as forced labour. Thousands of Australians were sent to build the Burma-Thailand Railway, cutting through jungle and rock mostly by hand.
Starvation, diseases such as cholera, overwork and beatings killed thousands of Australian prisoners. Many who survived had health problems long after the war.
version.remember: Singapore's surrender made thousands of Australians POWs, and thousands died from starvation, disease and brutality.

a.q: Why did about 15,000 Australians become prisoners of war in February 1942?
opts: Singapore was surrendered to Japanese forces
Their ships were sunk on the way to Singapore
Britain handed them to Japan in a peace deal
Japan won the war in the Pacific that month
a.why: On 15 February 1942 the British commander surrendered Singapore to Japan, and the Australians there were captured. There was no peace deal: Singapore was surrendered in battle.
a.clue: What happened to Singapore on 15 February 1942?

b.q: A historian reads the diary of an Australian POW on the Burma-Thailand Railway. Which entry fits what most prisoners there faced?
opts: Short of food again, and more men sick with cholera
Good meals today, and a doctor came to check on us
We were paid wages and sent letters home each week
Back in the front line, fighting the Japanese again
b.why: Prisoners on the railway did forced labour on little food, and diseases such as cholera killed many. Fighting in the front line does not fit, because POWs had been captured and were made to work, not fight.
b.clue: Think about how Japan treated its prisoners.

a.best: Singapore was surrendered to Japanese forces

b.best: Short of food again, and more men sick with cholera

check.summary: No problems found. The point is about the death and brutal treatment of prisoners of war, so it is marked as a sensitive topic.
